p.t: Financial distress is central to corporate finance and asset pricing. Standard structural models of risky debt imply that equity becomes riskier as firms approach default, and therefore that more financially distressed firms should earn higher expected equity returns (Merton, 1974;Leland, 1994). Yet the influential distress anomaly of Campbell, Hilscher and Szilagyi (2008) shows the opposite: more distressed firms earn lower subsequent stock returns. This paper revisits the distress anomaly from an industry perspective. We document a strong industry distress anomaly, show that it is neither a mechanical aggregation nor an artifact of the firm-level distress anomaly, and develop a quantitative industry equilibrium model in which financial distress affects expected returns through strategic competition and distress contagion among industry peers. 1The industry perspective is revealing because many firm-level anomalies weaken substantially after aggregation to the industry level. In contrast, the distress anomaly remains large and significant across four-digit SIC industries. Industries with higher financial distress earn lower subsequent equity returns. A long-short portfolio that buys high-distress industries and sells low-distress industries generates a negative and statistically significant return spread of 5.63% per year, which we refer to as the industry distress spread. This spread is comparable in magnitude to the traditional firm-level distress spread of about 8.5% per year after removing the industry component. The industry distress spread is not explained by the firm-level distress spread. It remains significant after controlling for the return spread generated by sorting firms on their own financial distress. Moreover, the industry distress spread disappears when we construct industry portfolios using synthetic industries formed by randomly reshuffling firms across actual industries, even though the synthetic industries are designed to match the distress risk of real industries. This distinction is central to our interpretation of the industry distress anomaly. If the anomaly merely reflected the aggregation of distressed firms, synthetic industries that preserve the distribution of firm-level distress should exhibit a similar distress-return relation. They do not. The disappearance of the spread in synthetic industries indicates that the relevant distress is not simply firm-idiosyncratic distress aggregated to the industry level. Instead, it is distress embedded in actual industry boundaries, where firms interact in product markets and share economically meaningful industry-specific characteristics. The industry distress anomaly therefore reflects a distinct industry-level force operating within actual product markets.

We argue that this force is a competition-distress feedback that explains the distressreturn relation across industries. When firms become financially distressed, shareholders place greater value on current cash flows relative to future gains from cooperation. Distressed firms therefore have stronger incentives to cut prices or margins to increase short-run revenue. More aggressive competition lowers profit margins for all firms in the industry, pushing them closer to default and further strengthening their incentives to compete aggressively. Financial distress thus intensifies competition, while intensified competition feeds back into greater financial distress. To formalize this idea, we develop a quantitative industry equilibrium model that embeds strategic competition into a dynamic model of long-term defaultable debt ('a la Leland, 1994). Firms sell differentiated products and compete repeatedly in profit margins. Consumers' tastes are summarized by firm-specific customer bases, which evolve stochastically and are subject to large idiosyncratic left-tail shocks, as in Seo and Wachter (2018). The customerbase structure is a key modeling ingredient. It captures not only the demand constraint generated by customer capital, as in Gourio and Rudanko (2014) and Dou et al. (2021b), but also the way customer capital shapes firms' effective demand elasticities (e.g., Dou, Ji and Wu, 2021). Cash flows depend on both customer bases and endogenous profit margins. Market leaders can tacitly sustain high margins, but each firm has an incentive to undercut its rivals to increase current revenue. Following the repeated-games literature, deviations are punished by a reversion to the non-collusive Nash outcome (e.g., Green and Porter, 1984;Brock and Scheinkman, 1985;Rotemberg and Saloner, 1986). The sustainable collusive margin is therefore determined by firms' deviation incentives, which depend on financial distress and aggregate discount rates.

The model links industry distress to expected returns through exposure to aggregate discount-rate shocks. When the aggregate discount rate rises, firms' continuation values fall. This has two effects. First, lower continuation values induce earlier default, increasing financial distress. Second, they reduce the value of future cooperation, weakening firms' ability to sustain collusive margins. Competition becomes more aggressive, profit margins fall, and distress rises further. The competition-distress feedback therefore amplifies the effect of discount-rate shocks on industry cash flows and equity values. The strength of this amplification differs systematically across industries. The key source of heterogeneity in our model is the idiosyncratic left-tail risk of firms' customer bases, which captures market leaders' exposure to large adverse idiosyncratic shocks to their customer bases, such as displacement by new technologies or rapidly expanding competitors (e.g., Gârleanu, Panageas and Yu, 2012;Kogan, Papanikolaou and Stoffman, 2020;Kogan et al., 2021). Because these shocks impair firms' future product-market positions, this default, and equity returns, building on the seminal frameworks of Merton (1974) and Leland (1994). A large literature studies how macroeconomic conditions affect capital structure, credit risk, and asset prices (e.g., Hackbarth, Miao and Morellec, 2006;Chen, Collin-Dufresne and Goldstein, 2008;Bhamra, Kuehn and Strebulaev, 2010a,b;Chen, 2010;Chen et al., 2018); how long-term debt interacts with corporate investment (e.g., Kuehn and Schmid, 2014;Gomes, Jermann and Schmid, 2016); how rollover risk affects credit risk and firm fundamentals (e.g., He and Xiong, 2012a,b); and how default decisions interact with secondary-market liquidity for corporate bonds (e.g., He and Milbradt, 2014;Chen et al., 2018). These models typically take product-market cash flows as exogenous to firms' financial distress or liquidity conditions. An exception is Corhay (2017), who develops structural credit models in which cash flows are shaped by non-collusive product-market competition. We instead study long-term defaultable debt in an industry equilibrium with tacit collusion. This allows financial distress and product-market competition to interact dynamically, generating joint predictions for equity returns, credit spreads, profitability, and industry distress.

Finally, our paper relates to the literature on industry competition, customer markets, and firm valuation. Early contributions by Titman (1984), Maksimovic (1988), and Titman and Wessels (1988) motivate a large literature on how product-market forces shape financial decisions. Empirically, Banerjee, Dasgupta and Kim (2008), Hoberg, Phillips and Prabhala (2014), and D' Acunto et al. (2018) study how industry competition and customer relationships affect leverage. Theoretically, a broad set of papers studies how industry competition and customer bases shape investment, cash holdings, mergers and acquisitions, entry, and exit (e.g., Dumas, 1989;Kovenock and Phillips, 1997;Grenadier, 2002;Aguerrevere, 2009;Back and Paulsen, 2009;Hoberg and Phillips, 2010;Hackbarth and Miao, 2012;Gourio and Rudanko, 2014;Hackbarth, Mathews and Robinson, 2014;Bustamante, 2015;Dou and Ji, 2021;Dou et al., 2021b). Closely related asset-pricing work studies how displacement risk and innovation affect incumbent firms' profits and risk exposures (e.g., Gârleanu, Kogan and Panageas, 2012;Kogan et al., 2017;Kogan, Papanikolaou and Stoffman, 2020), and how strategic competition and customer markets affect firm valuation and equity returns (e.g., Aguerrevere, 2009;Belo, Lin and Vitorino, 2014;Opp, Parlour and Walden, 2014;Bustamante, 2015;Belo et al., 2019;Corhay, Kung and Schmid, 2020;Dou et al., 2021b;Loualiche, 2021;Dou, Ji andWu, 2021, 2022;Lin, Ying and Zhang, 2025;Dou et al., 2026). These models primarily focus on all-equity firms or on equity valuation alone. We emphasize levered equity and credit spreads jointly, and show how their cross-sectional behavior is shaped by the dynamic feedback between endogenous competition and financial distress.

In this section, we provide evidence of the industry distress anomaly and show that it is an industry-level phenomenon, fundamentally distinct from the firm-level distress anomaly. Specifically, we first show that more distressed industries earn lower expected equity returns despite having higher credit spreads. We then find that less than half of the industry distress anomaly can be explained by the firm-level distress spread, suggesting that the two anomalies are likely driven by different economic mechanisms. Finally, we conduct placebo tests by reshuffling firms to construct synthetic industries that match actual industries on their industry-level characteristics. The cross-industry distress anomaly largely disappears in these reshuffled samples, suggesting that the effect is not merely a mechanical consequence of industry-level aggregation, but is instead tied to firms' strategic interactions within actual industries.

We obtain firm-level accounting data from Compustat and stock returns from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP). Industry-level stock returns are the average firm-level stock returns weighted by market capitalization. As in Chen et al. (2018), our credit spread data combine the Mergent Fixed Income Securities Database (FISD) from 1973 to 2004 and the Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine (TRACE) database from 2005 to 2018. We clean the Mergent FISD and TRACE data using the same procedures as in Collin-Dufresne, Goldstein and Martin (2001) and Dick-Nielsen (2009). Following Blanco, Brennan and Marsh (2005), we construct credit spreads as the difference between corporate bond yields and interest rate swap rates, which are regarded as the best parsimonious proxy for the risk-free rate (Feldhütter and Lando, 2008). The interest rate swap data are obtained from Bloomberg and are available starting in 1988. Our credit spread data are constructed for the period from 1988 to 2018 and cover a cross section of approximately 400 to 750 firms. We obtain credit default swap (CDS) spreads from Markit for the period from 2001 to 2018. Industrylevel credit spreads and CDS spreads are calculated as par-value-weighted averages of the corresponding firm-level spreads. For predictive analyses that combine market and annual accounting data, we follow Fama and French (1993) and assume that accounting information becomes available at the end of June each year. For quarterly accounting variables, we follow Campbell, Hilscher and Szilagyi (2008) and impose a two-month reporting lag based on the fiscal quarter-end month. Specifically, accounting variables for fiscal quarters ending in month m are first used in portfolios formed at the end of month m + 2, so that, for example, accounting variables for fiscal quarters ending in March are first used in portfolios formed at the end of May and matched to subsequent returns.

Our analysis focuses on strategic competition among leading oligopolistic firms within an industry that produce close substitutes. We define industries using SIC4 codes, following established practice in the literature. 3 We exclude all financial firms and utility firms, corresponding to SIC codes from 6,000 to 6,999 and from 4,900 to 4,999, respectively. Following the literature (e.g., Frésard, 2010), we also require that each industry-year observation include at least 10 firms to be retained in the analysis. 4 This requirement ensures that the industry-level variables are well behaved. On average, the sample contains 123 industries per year and 26.6 firms per industry. The firm distress measure for firm j in industry i and period t, denoted by Distress ij,t , is constructed as the 12-month failure probability, following Campbell, Hilscher and Szilagyi (2008). The industry distress measure for industry i in period t, denoted Distress i,t , is defined as the sales-weighted average of firm-level distress within the industry. 5 To construct the firm-level distress spread net of industry effects, we define the industry-adjusted firm distress measure, Ind_Adj_Distress ij,t . It is computed as the firm's distress minus the crosssectional average distress of all firms within the same industry in the same period. This construction is analogous to the "excess-industry" measure employed by Moskowitz and Grinblatt (1999) in forming industry-adjusted portfolios. Intuitively, the industry-adjusted measure removes cross-industry variation in financial distress and captures each firm's distress relative to its peers within the same industry.

To theoretically justify the industry component of the distress anomaly, we propose an industry equilibrium model with endogenous strategic competition. Our model essentially extends that of Leland (1994) by incorporating Bertrand competition between n firms with tacit collusion. For tractability, we assume that the industry has two dominant firms (n = 2), referred to as market leaders, and many followers of measure zero. We label a generic market leader by i and its competitor by j below.

Financial Frictions. Firms are financed by long-term debt and equity. For tractability, we model long-term debt as a consol with perpetual coupon payments at rate b i for firm i; further, we follow Leland (1994) and adopt a framework of static capital structure: the coupon rate b i is optimally chosen at the beginning upon the firm entering the market to maximize firm value given the tradeoff between tax shield benefits and distress costs. 7The corporate tax rate is τ > 0. A levered firm first uses its cash flows to make interest payments, then pays taxes, and finally distributes the rest to shareholders as dividends. The firm makes decisions to maximize its equity value. Shareholders have limited liability and the option to default on debt. When operating cash flows cannot cover interest expenses, the firm can issue equity to cover the shortfalls without paying any extra financing costs. When the equity value falls to zero, the firm will choose to file bankruptcy and exit. Upon exiting the market, the firm is sold as an intact business or is liquidated piecemeal, and its debtholders obtain a fraction ν of the asset value, with ν ∈ (0, 1). Cash Flows. Exploiting ex-ante heterogeneity in ν across industries, our model generates cross-industry variations in financial distress, profitability, and aggregate risk exposure.

We assume ζ > 0 to capture the well-documented countercyclical market price of risk. A primitive economic mechanism generating a countercyclical market price of risk is countercyclical variation in effective risk aversion, as in Campbell and Cochrane (1999). Interpretation of the Shocks. The aggregate Brownian shock Z t in equations ( 19) and ( 20) can be interpreted as the economy-wide or industry-wide demand shock. The shock ensures that variation in the discount rate γ t affects the valuation of firms' cash flows, and thus can generate variation in industry competition intensity. In other words, the aggregate demand shock Z t is needed for the discount-rate shock Z γ,t to affect valuation and competition intensity. The discount rate γ t is the only aggregate state variable. Economic downturns in our model are characterized by a high value of γ t .

The idiosyncratic Brownian shocks, W 1,t and W 2,t , can be interpreted as idiosyncratic demand (or taste) shocks. Idiosyncratic shocks are needed for the model to quantitatively match the default frequency and generate a nondegenerate cross-sectional distribution of the customer base in the stationary equilibrium. The idiosyncratic left-tail shocks, J 1,t and J 2,t , play a crucial role in our theory and empirical results. Idiosyncratic left-tail risk has been proven useful in explaining credit spreads and credit default swap index (CDX) spreads (e.g., Delianedis and Geske, 2001;Collin-Dufresne, Goldstein and Yang, 2012;Kelly, Manzo and Palhares, 2018;Seo and Wachter, 2018). We treat it as a crucial and fundamental industry characteristic in our model. We provide evidence that the heterogeneity in industry-level idiosyncratic left-tail risk ν is a crucial determinant for the cross-industry differences in financial distress. One interpretation of the idiosyncratic left-tail shock is that it captures exogenous displacement risk. Smaller firms continually challenge incumbent market leaders through distinctive innovation or rapid business expansion. Because such shocks impair firms' future product-market positions, this left-tail risk is a fundamental industry characteristic that cannot be substantially hedged by holding internal liquidity buffers such as cash. Changes in market leadership are often not gradual but rapid and disruptive (e.g., Christensen, 1997). For example, Apple and Samsung displaced Nokia and Motorola as market leaders in the mobile-phone industry within a relatively short period.

Exit and Entry: Endogenous Default versus Exogenous Displacement. In our model, a market leader can exit the industry in two ways, either endogenously or exogenously. On the one hand, market leader i can optimally choose to file bankruptcy and exit when its equity value drops to zero because of negative shocks to its customer base M i,t . This force leading to exit is similar to that of the standard Leland models through distance-to-default fluctuations. On the other hand, market leader i may go bankrupt and exit because of the occurrence of the idiosyncratic left-tail shock (i.e., dJ i,t = 1). This force leading to exit is similar to that of Seo and Wachter (2018) through "disastrous" idiosyncratic jump risk. We refer to the first way of exiting as endogenous default and the second as exogenous displacement. To maintain tractability, we assume that a new firm enters the industry only after an incumbent firm exits so that the number of firms stays constant. This assumption is inspired by the "return process" of Luttmer (2007) and the "exit and reinjection" assumption in the models of Miao (2005) and Gabaix et al. (2016) for industry dynamics. The same assumption is also commonly adopted in the IO literature on oligopolistic competition and predation (e.g., Besanko, Doraszelski and Kryukov, 2014) and is interpreted as the reorganization of the exiting firm. Essentially, the exit and reinjection assumption in our model implies that we always focus on the rivalry between the two top market leaders in the industry. In particular, upon incumbent firm i's exit, a new firm enters immediately with an initial customer base M new = κM j,0 > 0 and coupon rate b new , where b new is optimally chosen to maximize the new firm's value. The parameter κ > 0 captures the relative size of the new entrant and the initial size of the surviving incumbent, firm j. Upon entry, the dynamic game of Bertrand duopolistic competition, which we describe next in Section 3.3, is "reset" to a new one between the surviving incumbent firm and the new entrant.

The two firms in an industry play a supergame (Friedman, 1971), in which the stage games of setting profit margins are continuously played and infinitely repeated with exogenous and endogenous state variables varying over time. There exists a non-collusive equilibrium, which is the repetition of the one-shot Nash equilibrium, and thus is Markov perfect. In the collusive equilibrium, firms tacitly collude with each other in setting higher profit margins, where any deviation would trigger a switch to the noncollusive equilibrium. The collusion is "tacit" in the sense that it can be enforced without relying on legal contracts. Each firm is deterred from breaking the collusion agreement because doing so could provoke the fiercest competition (i.e., the non-collusive equilibrium in our model). Consider a generic collusive equilibrium in which the two firms follow a collusive profit-margin-setting scheme. Both firms can costlessly observe the other's profit margin, such that deviant behavior can be detected and punished. In this section, we conduct quantitative analysis. Subsection 4.1 describes the empirical measures. Subsection 4.2 calibrates the model's parameters. In Subsection 4.3, we study the model's implications on stock returns and credit spreads. Finally, in Subsection 4.4, we inspect the model's mechanism.

Measure of Discount Rate. Motivated by return predictability studies, the empirical proxy for discount rates is based on the smoothed earnings-price ratio (e.g., Campbell andShiller, 1988, 1998;Campbell and Thompson, 2008), which is obtained from Robert Shiller's website. Specifically, the discount rate in month t, denoted by Discount_rate t , is calculated by fitting a time-series regression of 12-month-ahead market returns to the smoothed earnings-price ratio and then taking the fitted value at the end of month t. We construct discount-rate shocks, denoted by ∆Discount_rate t , as the residuals of AR(1) time-series regressions, which are extracted at an annual or a quarterly frequency for the estimation of profit-margin betas and at a quarterly frequency for the estimation of equity and credit spread betas, aligning with the frequency of the beta-estimation regressions.

We retrieve and merge the information on Chapter 7 and Chapter 11 bankruptcies filed by large, public, nonfinancial U.S. firms over the period from 1981 to 2014 using the databases from New Generation Research's Bankruptcydata.com, the UCLA LoPucki Bankruptcy Research Database, Public Access to Court Electronic Records (PACER), National Archives at various locations, and U.S. Bankruptcy Courts for various districts, following Ma, Tong and Wang (2020) and Dou et al. (2021a). Similar to Campbell, Hilscher and Szilagyi (2008), we define a default event as the first of the following events: Chapter 7 or Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing, delisting due to insolvency (delisting code 572), and a default or selective default rating by a rating agency. This expanded measure of failure (relative to measuring only bankruptcy filings) allows us to capture instances in which firms fail but reach an agreement with creditors before an actual bankruptcy filing, such as pre-court liquidation or pre-court reorganization (e.g., Gilson, John and Lang, 1990;Gilson, 1997;Dou et al., 2021a).

In the model, an industry's default risk is determined by both its idiosyncratic left-tail risk and its distance to the default boundary. The crossindustry heterogeneity in default risk is mainly captured by industries' different levels of idiosyncratic left-tail risk, whereas the time-series variation in default risk within an industry is mainly reflected by the time-varying distance to default. Thus, we also construct a distance-to-default measure following the Merton model for the purpose of testing the competition-distress feedback effect. Specifically, we use (i) the book value of a firm's debt, computed as short-term debt plus one half of long-term debt, (ii) the total value of a firm's assets, estimated by the sum of the firm's book value of debt and its market value of equity, (iii) the risk-free rate, and (iv) the volatility of the market value of a firm's assets, approximated by the volatility of its deleveraged equity returns. The distance-todefault measure for industry i and period t, denoted by DD i,t , is the average firm-level distance-to-default measure of all firms in the same industry i weighted by their sales.

The model generates a high credit spread because both the risk premium and default boundaries are countercyclical in our model, the two ingredients that have been shown to be crucial to quantitatively match the credit spread in the data (Chen, Collin-Dufresne and Goldstein, 2008). We now quantitatively examine the asset pricing implications of the competition-distress feedback mechanism. Specifically, we show that our model can quantitatively rationalize the financial distress anomaly across industries: more financially distressed industries have lower expected equity excess returns and higher credit spreads. Panel A of Table 5 shows that in the data, the differences in expected equity excess returns and credit spreads between quintile portfolios of industries sorted on financial distress (Q5-Q1) are -5.63% and 2.35%, respectively. We perform the same portfolio sorting analyses in our model. The model-implied difference in expected equity excess returns (Q5-Q1) is -4.35%, which is comparable to the magnitude in the data. As discussed in Section 3.6, the difference in the idiosyncratic left-tail risk is the primary force causing the difference in financial distress across industries. Thus, sorting industries by financial distress in the model captures the cross-industry variation in idiosyncratic left-tail risk. Industries with higher financial distress have a weaker competition-distress feedback effect. As a result, these industries have lower expected equity excess returns because equity returns are less negatively exposed to aggregate discount-rate shocks (see panel B of Figure 4). The model-implied difference in credit spreads (Q5-Q1) is 1.81%, which is also comparable to the magnitude in the data. The model implies a positive difference in credit spreads because industries with higher idiosyncratic left-tail risk have a higher probability of default. This can be verified by looking at the 5-year default rate, which is 0.97% for Q1 and 4.94% for Q5. Similar patterns for default rates are also observed in the data. Therefore, the positive difference in credit spreads (Q5-Q1) is generated by the positive difference in default probabilities rather than the difference in credit risk premium. In fact, similar to the structural models following Merton (1974), the model-implied difference in credit risk premium (Q5-Q1) is negative, in line with the negative difference in expected equity excess returns (Q5-Q1). This implication is consistent with the empirical findings of Friewald, Wagner and Zechner (2014), who show that firms' excess equity returns are positively associated with their credit risk premia estimated from CDS spreads. Our model also implies that, compared with the industries in Q1, a larger proportion of the credit spreads of industries in Q5 is attributed to the higher default rates of these industries rather than the credit risk premia. This implication is consistent with the stylized fact documented by Huang and Huang (2012), that is, for firms with lower ratings (or higher credit spreads), expected default losses account for a larger fraction of their credit spreads than the credit risk premia.

In contrast to our model's implications, the canonical framework (e.g., Merton, 1974;Leland, 1994) cannot rationalize the financial distress anomaly. Specifically, we extend the standard model of Leland (1994) by incorporating the time-varying market price of risk (equations ( 20) and ( 21)). 19 This extended Leland framework implies higher expected returns and credit spreads for more financially distressed industries. This is because more financially distressed industries are closer to default and thus have higher financial leverage, which amplifies the exposure of both equity and debt to aggregate shocks. Unique to our model is that the competition-distress feedback mechanism, together with heterogeneous idiosyncratic left-tail risk, generates less negative exposure to the discount-rate shock and thus lower expected equity excess returns for the more financially distressed industries. In Online Appendix 1.3, we provide a decomposition of the risk premium and show that the cross-industry difference in expected equity excess returns is mainly due to the differential exposure to the discount-rate shock. Further, we emphasize that introducing idiosyncratic left-tail risk alone to the canonical framework does not help explain the industry distress anomaly. This is simply because idiosyncratic left-tail risk is not priced, so it merely increases the default rate without affecting the risk premium in the absence of the competition-distress feedback. This highlights the importance of the endogenous competition-distress feedback mechanism of our model. Idiosyncratic left-tail risk has cross-sectional asset pricing implications precisely because it affects the strength of the competition-distress feedback. The model also implies that the more financially distressed industries (Q5) have higher leverage ratios than the less financially distressed industries (Q1) because the former optimally choose higher financial leverage ex-ante. In our model, industries with higher financial distress are associated with a higher intensity of idiosyncratic left-tail shocks. Firms in such industries face weaker competition-distress feedback. Since the competition-distress feedback is an additional source of financial distress costs for issuing debt, a weaker feedback effect implies lower distress costs and thus a higher optimal leverage ratio. Moreover, the model implies that the more financially distressed industries (Q5) have lower profit margins than the less financially distressed industries (Q1), and the difference in magnitude is similar to that in the data. Thus, the model rationalizes the negative profitability-leverage relationship across industries in the data. Panel B of Table 5 further strengthens the empirical support for our mechanism by sorting industries based on their idiosyncratic left-tail risk in both the data and the model. 20The patterns are similar to those in panel A of Table 5 because the cross-industry variation in financial distress is mainly determined by the cross-industry difference in idiosyncratic left-tail risk. By contrast, we examine the hypothetical industries constructed in Section 2.4 and show that the differences in expected equity excess returns across the quintile portfolios of hypothetical industries sorted on idiosyncratic left-tail risk are statistically insignificant (see panel C of Table IA.V in Online Appendix 2.4).

In Table 6, we conduct various counterfactual experiments with the aim of examining the model's mechanism. Column (3) of Table 6 presents the model's implications in the non-collusive equilibrium. Because the endogenous competition-distress feedback is absent, firms choose a higher initial leverage, leading to a higher leverage ratio, compared with the collusive equilibrium. For the same reason, the equity premium and credit spread of the market portfolio decrease from 7.02% and 1.51% to 3.67% and 1.29%, respectively. More importantly, the difference in expected equity excess returns of portfolios sorted on financial distress (Q5-Q1) becomes positive with a small magnitude because the crossindustry difference in ν does not affect industries' profit margins or their exposure to the discount rate in the non-collusive equilibrium. The positive excess return difference (Q5-Q1) reflects the higher financial leverage of more financially distressed industries (Q5). The comparison between collusive and non-collusive outcomes indicates that the competitiondistress feedback mechanism is the key to explaining the industry distress anomaly in our model. However, the credit spread remains significantly different between the portfolios sorted on financial distress or idiosyncratic left-tail risk due to the cross-industry difference in default risk. To illustrate the importance of the cross-industry difference in idiosyncratic left-tail risk, in column (4), we assume that all industries have the same intensity of idiosyncratic left-tail shocks, ν ≡ (ν + ν)/2. Not surprisingly, the model implies that both the equity premium and the credit spread are similar across industry portfolios sorted on idiosyncratic left-tail risk. The small and positive excess return difference (Q5-Q1) for industry portfolios sorted on financial distress reflects a pure leverage effect. In column (5) of Table 6, we evaluate the model's quantitative implications for ϵ = 3. The competition-distress feedback effect weakens as the cross-industry price elasticity of demand ϵ is larger, because a larger ϵ makes it more difficult to collude (Dou, Ji and Wu, 2021). As the feedback effect is weaker, the average equity premium and credit spread of the market portfolio decrease from 7.02% and 1.51% (column 2) to 6.28% and 1.32% (column 5), respectively. The model-implied difference in expected equity excess returns and credit spreads between industries with high and low financial distress (or idiosyncratic left-tail risk) also becomes less pronounced.

The strength of the competition-distress feedback mechanism also depends on the gap between η and ϵ. If η = ϵ, firms are effectively engaging in monopolistic competition, leaving no room for collusion on higher profit margins. Column (6) of Table 6 shows that changing η to 12 reduces the equity premium and credit spread, as well as their cross-industry differences.

We provide empirical evidence for the model in three steps. Subsection 5.1 provides evidence showing that the industry-level idiosyncratic left-tail risk is a fundamental industry characteristic that explains the industry distress anomaly. Subsection 5.2 provides evidence for the economic mechanism that explains the industry distress anomaly. Subsection 5.3 tests the competition-distress feedback mechanism.

p.s: Idiosyncratic Left-Tail Risk and Financial Distress Anomaly
p.t: In Subsection 5.1.1, we examine the relationship among industry-level idiosyncratic left-tail risk, financial distress, and profit margin. In Subsection 5.1.2, we show that the industry-level distress spread becomes statistically insignificant after controlling for the industry-level idiosyncratic left-tail risk.

p.s: Idiosyncratic Left-Tail Risk, Financial Distress, and Profit Margin
p.t: Our model predicts that the idiosyncratic left-tail risk is negatively associated with the profit margin due to the competition-distress feedback mechanism and positively associated with the level of financial distress across industries (see Figure 4 and Table 5). To empirically examine this relationship, we sort all SIC4 industries into quintiles based on the industrylevel measure of idiosyncratic left-tail risk (ν i,t ). The average financial distress and profit margins of quintile group Q5 (high ν i,t ) minus those of quintile group Q1 (low ν i,t ) are 0.11% and -11.57%, respectively. The differences are also statistically significant as the t-statistics robust to heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation are 8.36 and -6.70, respectively. Therefore, industries with high ν i,t are indeed associated with higher financial distress and lower profit margins than those with low ν i,t . Further, we conduct similar sorting analyses based on the hypothetical industries constructed in Section 2.4, where the idiosyncratic left-tail risk of each hypothetical industry is re-estimated following the same procedure in Section 4.1. Panel A of Table IA.V in Online Appendix 2.4 shows that the difference (Q5-Q1) in distress across hypothetical industries is no longer statistically significant, and its magnitude is much lower than that across real industries. This implies that, rather than a firm characteristic, the idiosyncratic left-tail risk is a fundamental industry characteristic that is correlated with industry-level distress across real industries. Thus, the variation in idiosyncratic left-tail risk captures the variation in financial distress across real industries, but not hypothetical industries. Moreover, panel B of Table IA.V in Online Appendix 2.4 shows that the difference (Q5-Q1) in profit margins across hypothetical industries is no longer statistically significant, and its magnitude is much lower than that across real industries. This suggests that the mechanism that generates the negative relation between idiosyncratic left-tail risk and profit margins only exists in real industries, but not in hypothetical industries. As demonstrated by our model, this mechanism is the competition-distress feedback, which captures distressed firms' competition behavior within the same real industry, but not the same hypothetical industry. Intuitively, firms within the same hypothetical industry are not directly competing with each other in the product market. This explains the lack of statistically significant correlations between profit margins and idiosyncratic left-tail risk across hypothetical industries in the data.

p.s: Industry Distress Anoamly After Controlling For ν i,t
p.t: Building on the results presented in Table 5, we further investigate whether the industry-level distress spread significantly diminishes after controlling for the industry-level idiosyncratic left-tail risk. We perform a double-sort analysis, where we first sort industries into quintiles based on the measure of idiosyncratic left-tail risk (ν i,t ). Then, for industries within each quintile portfolio, we further sort them into quintiles based on the industry distress measure (Distress i,t ). Panel A of Table 7 reports the results. The magnitude of the differences (Q5-Q1) in expected equity excess returns and the alphas of CAPM and the Fama-French three-factor model are -2.326%, -2.848%, and -2.987%, respectively, which are statistically insignificant, as compared with -5.625%, -8.165%, and -9.683% in panel A of Table 1. Panel B of Table 7 performs an additional test by sorting industries on an adjusted industry distress measure (Distress_adjusted i,t ) which controls for idiosyncratic left-tail risk ν i,t . Specifically, Distress_adjusted i,t is the residuals of regressing the industry distress measure (Distress i,t ) on the measure of idiosyncratic left-tail risk (ν i,t ) and a constant term in the cross section of industries in each month t. It is evident that both the differences (Q5-Q1) in expected equity excess returns and the alphas of CAPM and the Fama-French three-factor model become statistically insignificant once we sort industries on Distress_adjusted i,t .

p.s: Industry Distress Anoamly After Controlling For ν i,t
p.t: Taken together, the empirical findings support our model's prediction that the crossindustry heterogeneity in financial distress is mainly captured by industries' different levels of idiosyncratic left-tail risk, which is a fundamental industry characteristic that explains the industry distress anomaly.

p.s: Economic Mechanism Behind the Industry Distress Anomaly
p.t: According to the model, the economic mechanism that generates the industry-level distress spread is the industries' differential exposure to discount-rate shocks (i.e., Z γ,t ). We now provide empirical tests for this mechanism. Specifically, in Subsection 5.2.1, we show that industries with higher financial distress or idiosyncratic left-tail risk are less negatively exposed to discount-rate shocks. In Subsection 5.2.2, we show that the industry-level discount-rate spread, i.e., the equity returns of the long-short portfolio of industries sorted on their expected loadings on discount-rate shocks, strongly comoves with the industrylevel distress spread. Furthermore, the industry-level distress spread becomes statistically insignificant after controlling for the industry-level discount-rate spread. In Subsection 5.2.3, we show that the industry-level discount-rate spread and the industry-level distress spread have similar explanatory power for the cross-sectional equity returns of portfolios that vary in the level of distress risk.

p.s: Feedback Effect on Profit Margins and Equity Returns
p.t: We first test the feedback effect on profit margins. Our model implies that industry-level profit margins load negatively on the discount rate, and more so in industries where firms are closer to their default boundaries (see panel C of Figure 3), because the strength of the competition-distress feedback effect increases as firms approach their default boundaries. To test this implication, we sort industries into different groups based on the distanceto-default measure (DD i,t ). We then examine the profit-margin beta to the discount rate by running the following time-series regression using yearly observations for each group k: where the dependent variable ∆ ln(1 + PM k,t ) ≡ ln(1 + PM k,t )ln(1 + PM k,t-1 ) is the year-on-year change in group-k's net profit margin measure ln(1 + PM k,t ), which is the equal-weighted average of logged one plus the industry-level net profit margin of all industries in group k. 23Panel A of Table 10 presents the results. p.s: Feedback Effect on Profit Margins and Equity Returns
p.t: We further test the feedback effect on equity returns. As shown in Figure 4, the competition-distress feedback is stronger when industries are closer to the default boundary. As a result, the difference in the equity beta to the discount rate across industries with different gross profitability widens when the distance to default is lower. As shown in Figure 4 and Table 5, the asset-pricing implications of our model are generated by industries' differential exposure to aggregate discount-rate shocks owing to the differences in the strength of the competition-distress feedback across industries. The competition-distress feedback becomes weaker when industries' market structure becomes more competitive. In this section, we provide direct evidence supporting this mechanism. Properly measuring market structure changes in our panel regressions is challenging. Endogeneity problems will arise if we use empirical proxies for the competitiveness of market structure such as the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI). Specifically, omitted variables that are correlated with both changes in HHI and the feedback effect could exist through channels other than the competitiveness of market structure. For instance, technology development can lead to both changes in HHI and changes in the sensitivity of industries' profit margins to the discount rate by altering the duration of firms' cash flows. To address the endogeneity concern, we exploit exogenous variation in the competitiveness of market structure at the industry level. We follow the literature (Frésard, 2010;Valta, 2012;Frésard and Valta, 2016;Dou, Ji and Wu, 2021) and use unexpected large cuts in import tariffs to identify exogenous variation in market structures. The existing literature provides extensive evidence showing that tariff cuts substantially alter the competitive configuration of industries. For example, Bernard, Jensen and Schott (2006) show that import tariff cuts significantly increase competitive pressures from foreign rivals. Valta (2012) shows that tariff reductions are followed by a significant increase in imports.

This paper documents the industry distress anomaly and provides a risk-based explanation. In the data, we show that the distress anomaly is significant across both firms and industries. However, the industry-level distress spread cannot be fully explained by the firm-level distress spread, suggesting that the industry-and firm-level distress anomalies could be driven by different economic mechanisms. Moreover, the industry-level distress spread is no longer significant in hypothetical industries, suggesting that it is tied to some economic mechanism within real industries, with its strength depending on certain industry characteristics. To provide a structural explanation for the industry distress anomaly, we develop a dynamic model of long-term defaultable debt that incorporates time-varying discount rates and a supergame of strategic rivalry. Our model shows that the competition-distress feedback within industries amplifies industries' exposure to aggregate discount-rate shocks, more so for less distressed industries that feature a low level of idiosyncratic left-tail risk. As such, our model provides a novel mechanism that helps explain the puzzling crossindustry patterns of equity and bond returns, namely, the industry distress anomaly -more distressed industries exhibit lower expected equity returns despite having higher credit spreads.
